newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Russia backs anti-personnel landmine talks.
newsitem.headline: Russia backs anti-personnel landmine talks.

text.p: Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov on Thursday backed launching negotiations in the Conference on Disarmament for a global ban on anti-personnel landmines, but said it should probably be a phased ban.
In a speech, he also urged the 61-member body to break its impasse and start talks to ban production of bomb-making fissile material as the next step in multilateral nuclear disarmament.

The United Nations-sponsored body has yet to adopt its 1997 work programme due to a row between the five declared nuclear weapons states and non-aligned countries, led by India, over what its priorities should be in the nuclear area.

The United States and other Western states are pushing hard to go ahead with negotiations for a global ban on landmines. The lethal weapons are blamed for killing 25,000 people a year and maiming more, mainly civilians.

The talks would be parallel to Canada's "Ottawa Process", but diplomats say they would mean more as both China and Russia -- major producers and users of landmines -- are members of the Geneva forum. Neither participates fully in the Canadian effort which aims to reach a ban among 50 countries by year-end.

"We share the concern of the international community about their irresponsible use," Primakov said, adding that Moscow was considering extending its December 1994 moratorium on exports of non-self-destructible and undetectables mines.
"We consider the complete ban on anti-personnel land mines as a goal, the movement towards which should probably consist of a number of agreed time stages," he added.
Primakov offered no timetable for a phased ban, but said the Conference on Disarmament included "the main states concerned".
"He made clear Russia's desire to get work started on mines in the Conference and to maintain it as a forum," one Western diplomat said. "But we have no idea of Russia's timetable."

Britain's new Labour government last month pledged to destroy all of the country's landmines by 2005 and said it would observe a moratorium on their use until that year or until an effective international ban was clinched.
Western diplomats blame a handful of states -- including Cuba, Syria, Mexico, Morocco, and Nigeria -- for joining forces to block progress in Geneva on mines.
"Some countries don't want to deal with the anti-personnel landmines problem. They have important internal, national security concerns," said one Western diplomat.
"Cuba and Syria are the main problems, but Nigeria and Morocco are also trying to block it," he added.
Western states hope a special coordinator can be named to hold intensive consultations with all members in a bid to reach consensus on a mandate for negotiations on mines.
Western countries also argue that the next priority in the nuclear field should be negotiations to halt production of fissile material (plutonium and highly-enriched uranium).

Non-aligned countries, led by India, are insisting the five declared nuclear weapon states (Britain, China, France, Russia, and the United States) agree to launch talks in Geneva aimed at the total elimination of nuclear weapons by the year 2005. Only then would the non-aligned agree to launch fissile talks.
The nuclear powers have refused the demand for talks on total disarmament, saying cuts in nuclear stockpiles are being made in a bilateral context between Washington and Moscow.
"Ensuring continuous dynamic development of the disarmament processes is a historic task," Primakov said. "Any pause in this sphere, especially a protracted one, may entail a set-back.

"As to the immediate tasks faced by the Conference on Disarmament, we believe that in the nuclear sphere they include a ban on production of fissionable materials for nuclear weapons or other nuclear devices.
"We are ready for the prompt beginning of negotiations on this issue here, in the multilateral forum on disarmament."
